paras: The killing of Billy Gill took place in the Indian Territory near Woodward about April 6, 1888, when a party of some two dozen men from southern Kansas pursued Gill, whom they accused of stealing their horses, and shot him dead. No arrest or inquest was reported. Papers from Kansas to Georgia carried the news, treating Gill as a notorious desperado, and one dispatch linked his killers to vigilance committees that meant to execute horse thieves without trial.

According to a Woodward special printed in mid-April, a large band of horse thieves had made its headquarters in the neutral strip known as "No Man's Land" and raided the border towns of southern Kansas for cattle and horses. The same dispatch said the farmers, "incensed" by the raids, had organized vigilance committees to rid themselves of the thieves. Gill was described as a "notorious desperado" who had served time in the Kansas penitentiary, two terms by the Little Rock account. That account added that he kept stolen horses at a secluded spot on the Washita river and had operated in Missouri, Arkansas and Kansas.

Gill was accused of taking horses in Kansas, six by most accounts and five in the Little Rock version, with the help of accomplices. The owners and their neighbors followed him into the Indian Territory. A Kansas City Times special dated April 7 said twenty-three men from the vicinity of Ashland, Kansas, overtook him ten miles from Woodward "yesterday" and "riddled him with bullets." The Woodward special instead put the party at about twenty-five men from near Coldwater, Kansas, and the place at fifteen miles from Woodward, and said Gill had the horses in his possession "at the time he was captured."

Advices from Little Rock gave a third version, in which over twenty pursuers, among them the owners of the horses, shot him fifteen miles beyond Woodward because he "refused to surrender." No report names any of the pursuers or any officer with them, although the Little Rock dispatch called the party "a posse."

The coverage shows no arrest, inquest or other official response to the killing. The Woodward special reported that armed parties were "continually passing and repassing" the town on the lookout for horse thieves and would "enforce the death penalty without trial" on any they caught.

The Kansas City Times dispatch reached the wire on April 7 and 8 and ran under headlines such as "BILLY GILL KILLED" in the Wichita Eagle, "A Desperado Killed" in the Savannah Morning News and "Riddled With Bullets" in the St. Paul Daily Globe. Shorter items in news-summary columns followed, including the San Antonio Daily Light's line that Gill "has been caught and shot" and a one-sentence notice in the Macon Beacon. In Kansas the Barbour County Index of Medicine Lodge reported that he had been killed "by a pursuing party from Ashland."

A week later the Woodward special appeared in weekly papers in Michigan and Dakota, among them the True Northerner, the Crawford Avalanche, the Turner County Herald and the Wessington Springs Herald, which printed it twice in one issue. There it was bundled with an unrelated Oklahoma report of a battle with Black horse thieves and the hanging of four others, all under the headline "HORSE THIEVES LYNCHED." The Little Rock version, which called Gill "a notorious horse thief" and said he was believed to have stolen five hundred horses, ran in Ohio papers under "The Champion Horse Thief Killed" and "A Desperado Finally Gets His Dues." None of these reports questioned the killing, and none stated Gill's race.

The accounts differ on the pursuers' home town (Ashland or Coldwater), their number (twenty-three, about twenty-five, or over twenty), the distance from Woodward (ten or fifteen miles) and the number of horses (six or five). They also differ on how he died: the Woodward special implies he was captured, while the Little Rock version says he was shot for refusing to surrender. The April 7 Kansas City dispatch is the closest in time to the event and places it on April 6, which was a Friday, consistent with the Little Rock advices' "Friday last."

reader.title: Killing of Billy Gill
bases: A party of about two dozen private men from southern Kansas, described in one dispatch as members of vigilance committees, pursued a man accused of stealing their horses into the Indian Territory and shot him dead (A1, A13, A18).

Twenty-three to twenty-five men with no reported legal authority, organized as vigilance committees intending 'the death penalty without trial' for horse thieves, shot Gill over stolen horses (A1, A13). It is probable rather than certain because the Little Rock version says he was shot when he refused to surrender, a resisting-pursuit killing, while the Woodward special says he was 'captured' (A13, A18).

Three separately datelined reports (a Kansas City Times special from Woodward, a later Woodward special, and Little Rock advices) and a Kansas local brief agree that a pursuing party from southern Kansas shot Gill near Woodward over stolen horses (A1, A5, A13, A18).

framing.detail: Reports called Gill a 'notorious desperado' and 'champion horse thief', and the Hillsboro News-Herald headed the story 'A Desperado Finally Gets His Dues'.
Most papers ran the Kansas City wire or the Woodward special without comment, the latter under the bundle headline 'HORSE THIEVES LYNCHED'.

conflicts.note: The two Kansas towns are named in separate dispatches; the Barbour County Index, a Kansas paper, follows the Ashland version.
April 6, 1888 was a Friday, so the two agree if the Little Rock advices were older than their dateline; the April 7 dispatch is the closer source.
